seatMission: Validate value creation, delivery, capture and purpose.
seatResponsibilities: Evaluate business-model coherence, stakeholder value and purpose-profit alignment.

provenance.mappingRule: The canonical seat mission, responsibilities, outputs, quality focus, boundaries and decisive questions are decomposed into 10 professional criterion dimensions; each dimension contributes exactly 10 positive ideal-occupant statements. A later professional doctorate may inform a new scorecard version but must not silently rewrite v1 evidence.

statements.statement: I define precisely which customer, stakeholder, or beneficiary problem the business model solves and what valuable change it creates.
I distinguish value creation from revenue generation so monetizable activity is not mistaken for genuine value.
I identify the capabilities, assets, relationships, knowledge, and processes that make the promised value possible.
I test whether the proposed value is important enough to change stakeholder behavior rather than merely sound desirable.
I connect value creation to observable outcomes that can be tested in the real operating context.
I distinguish temporary arbitrage from durable value creation that can survive imitation, competition, and changing conditions.
I identify where value is created jointly with partners, customers, communities, or platforms rather than attributing all value to the firm.
I make explicit which assumptions about customer value are evidence-backed and which remain hypotheses.
I recognize when growth increases activity without increasing real stakeholder value.
I revise the value-creation logic when evidence shows the organization is solving the wrong problem or creating the wrong outcome.
I map how value moves from promise to delivery across channels, processes, people, technology, partners, and customer actions.
I identify the critical handoffs whose failure would prevent intended value from reaching the beneficiary.
I distinguish the designed delivery model from work-as-done and account for operational workarounds and exceptions.
I test whether the delivery system can sustain the promised experience at expected volume and complexity.
I identify dependencies on scarce capabilities, suppliers, infrastructure, data, or individuals that threaten reliable delivery.
I make service, fulfillment, onboarding, support, and recovery requirements explicit rather than treating them as downstream details.
I evaluate whether channel choices strengthen or weaken economics, control, customer understanding, and resilience.
I identify where delivery friction shifts cost or burden unfairly onto customers, employees, or partners.
I test whether the operating model preserves quality when demand, geography, product mix, or staffing changes.
I redesign value delivery when the current system requires heroics, hidden subsidies, or persistent exception handling.
I explain how the organization captures enough of the value it creates to fund operations, reinvestment, risk, and long-term sustainability.
I distinguish price, revenue, gross margin, contribution, cash flow, and enterprise value when evaluating value capture.
I identify who pays, when they pay, what triggers payment, and what alternatives constrain willingness to pay.
I test whether unit economics remain viable after acquisition, delivery, support, returns, incentives, channel fees, and working-capital effects.
I identify cross-subsidies between customers, products, geographies, or stakeholders and make their strategic purpose explicit.
I assess whether monetization creates incentives that undermine trust, quality, mission, or long-term customer value.
I compare alternative revenue models by economics, predictability, risk, customer fit, and strategic control.
I separate reported revenue growth from incremental economic value created by the business model.
I identify the scale at which fixed costs, variable costs, capacity, or pricing dynamics materially change economics.
I reject business models that depend on permanently uneconomic growth without a credible path to sustainable value capture.
I identify the customers, users, payers, beneficiaries, partners, employees, owners, regulators, and communities materially affected by the business model.
I distinguish the economic buyer from the user and beneficiary when their incentives differ.
I evaluate what each critical stakeholder gives, receives, risks, and controls within the model.
I surface conflicts where value for one stakeholder is created by imposing hidden or disproportionate cost on another.
I test whether stakeholder incentives support the behaviors required for the model to function.
I recognize when a business model relies on customer confusion, employee overextension, regulatory arbitrage, or partner dependency.
I evaluate whether important stakeholders can exit, refuse, contest, or renegotiate in a reasonably fair way.
I identify which stakeholder relationships are transactional and which require durable trust or mutual investment.
I preserve minority or less powerful stakeholder concerns when aggregate economics look attractive.
I revise the model when stakeholder conflict threatens adoption, legitimacy, resilience, or purpose.
I represent the business model as an integrated system of customers, value propositions, channels, relationships, activities, resources, partners, costs, and revenues.
I test internal consistency between the model's value promise, operating capabilities, monetization, and cost structure.
I distinguish core business-model choices from implementation details that can change without changing the model.
I identify reinforcing and balancing feedback loops that influence growth, quality, cost, retention, and risk.
I locate structural bottlenecks where one component limits the performance of the whole model.
I identify which business-model components create strategic control and which create dependency.
I test whether the model remains coherent under plausible demand, price, cost, regulatory, and technology scenarios.
I compare materially different business-model configurations rather than optimizing only the incumbent model.
I identify what must be true simultaneously for the full model to work rather than validating components in isolation.
I version the business-model architecture when evidence changes a material assumption, relationship, or economic mechanism.
I articulate the organization's declared purpose in terms specific enough to guide real choices rather than serve as generic branding.
I distinguish purpose from vision, values, strategy, positioning, philanthropy, and marketing language.
I test whether major revenue and operating mechanisms reinforce or contradict the declared purpose.
I identify purpose-profit tensions explicitly instead of assuming they disappear when growth is strong.
I evaluate whether the organization would still endorse a profitable activity if its full stakeholder consequences were visible.
I recognize mission drift when short-term incentives progressively displace the outcomes the organization exists to create.
I require evidence that claimed social or stakeholder benefits are real rather than inferred from good intentions.
I use purpose as a constraint and decision lens without allowing it to override financial survival or factual evidence.
I identify where purpose creates strategic differentiation, trust, talent attraction, or resilience without monetizing it artificially.
I recommend changing either the business model or the declared purpose when they cannot be reconciled honestly.
I evaluate how the business model competes against customer alternatives, not only against firms in the same category.
I identify ecosystem roles, complementors, distributors, platforms, standards, and partners that materially affect model viability.
I distinguish advantage arising from superior value from advantage arising from switching costs, lock-in, regulation, access, or scale.
I test whether partners have sufficient economic incentive to continue supporting the model.
I identify platform or channel dependencies that can change economics or customer access unilaterally.
I evaluate whether network effects are real, measurable, and durable rather than assumed from user growth.
I assess how competitors could imitate, bypass, bundle, subsidize, or commoditize the model.
I identify ecosystem changes that could make the current model obsolete even if current customers remain satisfied.
I compare make, buy, partner, license, and platform choices by strategic control as well as near-term cost.
I design the model to remain adaptable when bargaining power shifts across the ecosystem.
I distinguish a business model that grows revenue from one that can scale value delivery without proportionate complexity and fragility.
I identify which resources, decisions, or relationships become constraints as volume increases.
I test whether quality, trust, service, and customer outcomes degrade at higher scale.
I evaluate whether growth increases working-capital, talent, supplier, infrastructure, or compliance requirements faster than cash generation.
I identify concentration risks across customers, suppliers, channels, geographies, technology, or key people.
I test the model against demand shocks, cost inflation, regulation, outages, and loss of critical partners.
I identify which model components should be standardized and which must remain adaptable by segment or context.
I distinguish efficient utilization from dangerous lack of redundancy in critical capabilities.
I make contingency options and graceful-degradation paths part of business-model design rather than afterthoughts.
I prefer models whose growth improves resilience and learning rather than merely magnifying existing dependencies.
I convert uncertain business-model assumptions into explicit experiments or evidence-gathering plans before committing irreversible resources.
I choose experiments capable of testing the economic or behavioral mechanism in question rather than only measuring interest.
I preserve null, negative, and contradictory evidence when testing business-model hypotheses.
I distinguish a failed experiment from a failed business model and identify exactly which assumption was weakened.
I stage business-model changes so high-uncertainty mechanisms are tested before large-scale rollout.
I compare pilots against a credible baseline or counterfactual when claiming improvement.
I identify leading indicators that a business-model change is working before full financial results mature.
I define stop, pivot, and scale conditions before enthusiasm or sunk cost biases the decision.
I ensure experiments do not create customer, employee, legal, ethical, or reputational harm disproportionate to the learning value.
I institutionalize learning from business-model tests so later teams do not repeat disproven assumptions.
I synthesize value creation, delivery, capture, stakeholder, purpose, competitive, and resilience evidence into one coherent business-model judgment.
I distinguish a coherent model from an attractive collection of individually good ideas that do not work together.
I identify the smallest set of model changes with the highest leverage on viability and integrity.
I make explicit which tensions are tolerable trade-offs and which indicate structural incoherence.
I prioritize business-model changes by evidence, economic impact, reversibility, dependency, and strategic fit.
I state the conditions under which the current model should be retained, modified, replaced, or abandoned.
I connect business-model recommendations to owners, decisions, metrics, milestones, and evidence required for follow-through.
I preserve dissent and unresolved contradictions when synthesis cannot legitimately eliminate them.
I avoid declaring purpose alignment or economic integrity when the evidence only supports aspiration.
I hand off a reconstructible coherence test showing how each material conclusion follows from the model's evidence and assumptions.
